title: Perry v. Sindermann
lead: A Texas professor alleges that years of institutional assurances and his public criticism matter despite annual contracts; the Court requires an opportunity to prove both theories.

actors.name: Robert Sindermann
actors.role: Government and Social Science professor at Odessa Junior College.

actors.name: Odessa’s Regents and president
actors.role: Officials denying renewal and defending their decision.

proceedings: The district court entered summary judgment for the college officials.
The Fifth Circuit reversed and remanded for consideration of speech and employment-expectancy claims.
The Supreme Court affirmed the remand but required an objectively supported entitlement, not subjective expectancy.
limits: The sparse summary-judgment record did not establish retaliation, tenure, or a successful liberty claim. The Court ordered no reinstatement or damages. Powell did not participate.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Sindermann builds a teaching career under annual contracts
sections.cue: What assurances did he claim beyond the contract’s end date?
paragraphs: Robert Sindermann taught in Texas public colleges from 1959 to 1969: two years at the University of Texas, four at San Antonio Junior College, and four at Odessa Junior College. From 1965 Odessa employed him through successive one-year contracts to teach Government and Social Science; he served for a time as department cochairman. Long service supplied context, not automatic tenure.

Odessa had no formal tenure system. Its Faculty Guide nevertheless said the administration wished teachers to feel permanently tenured while their teaching remained satisfactory, their attitude toward colleagues and superiors cooperative, and they remained happy in their work. Sindermann alleged that the college promulgated that assurance and fostered reliance on it. He also invoked statewide coordinating-board guidelines generally contemplating no more than seven years’ appropriate full-time probationary service, with qualifications, and continued tenure employment absent adequate cause. Whether those guidelines bound Odessa and which years counted remained to be proved.

sections.title: Public disagreement precedes nonrenewal
sections.cue: Which explanation for the Regents’ action remained contested?
paragraphs: In 1968–1969 Sindermann became president of the Texas Junior College Teachers Association, testified before legislative committees, and opposed positions of Odessa’s Regents. He supported transforming Odessa into a four-year institution, which the Regents opposed, and a newspaper advertisement bearing his name criticized them. Officials alleged that some legislative appearances violated instructions not to leave his classes. Protected criticism and asserted insubordinate conduct were therefore competing accounts, not findings already reconciled.

When his contract ended in May 1969, the Regents voted against renewal. They issued a press release charging insubordination but supplied no official statement of reasons and no hearing to contest the decision. A public accusation was part of the record; it was neither a completed hearing nor a Supreme Court finding that his liberty claim had succeeded.

Sindermann sued the Regents and college president in federal court, claiming speech retaliation and denial of due process. Officials relied on the contract’s expiration and absence of formal tenure. The summary-judgment record held pleadings and three short Sindermann affidavits substantially repeating his allegations; the officials submitted none. The district court nevertheless held that expiration and lack of tenure defeated a cause of action.

sources.pinpoint: Material Facts; Procedural History; 408 U.S. 594–596 & nn.1–4

sections.title: The appellate courts reopen two different constitutional routes
sections.cue: Why did the speech claim survive without a guaranteed future job?
paragraphs: The Fifth Circuit reversed and remanded. It required a judicial hearing on the disputed motive and examination of an expectancy of continued employment. Justice Stewart’s five-Justice Supreme Court opinion agreed that the case must return, while qualifying what kind of expectancy counted.

Government may have discretion to deny a benefit for many reasons but cannot withhold it to penalize protected speech. It cannot indirectly impose a penalty it could not impose directly. The Court had applied that principle to public employment and annual contracts of nontenured teachers. Sindermann therefore did not need to establish entitlement to another job before challenging a retaliatory reason.

That rule did not prove retaliation. The Court did not classify every criticism as protected in every context or find insubordination pretextual. Legislative testimony and criticism of public college policy presented a bona fide constitutional issue under precedents protecting teachers’ public-concern speech. The actual motive remained disputed and undeveloped; lack of tenure alone could not support summary judgment.

sections.title: The Faculty Guide may support property, but its legal effect needs proof
sections.cue: What makes an assurance different from an employee’s hope?
paragraphs: Procedural due process required its own showing of liberty or property. Losing one job or alleging retaliation did not automatically create an administrative hearing right. As in Board of Regents v. Roth, the companion public-employment case, the relevant property inquiry concerned independent rules or mutually explicit understandings supporting legitimate entitlement.

The Faculty Guide combined denial of formal tenure with language suggesting security under stated conditions. Neither part conclusively settled the relationship. Sindermann could attempt to prove an institutional understanding from words, conduct, surrounding circumstances, and past usage. Ordinary contract principles recognize that formal text may not exhaust a relationship. An institution using annual contracts even for senior faculty could develop a common law of tenure-like security, but repeated appointments did not create a federal guarantee of perpetual renewal.

State law remained decisive. The Court expressly stated that the theory would fail if Texas law gave a teacher in Sindermann’s position no contractual or other tenure claim. His decade of service and coordinating-board guidelines were possible evidence, not conclusive promises. The Constitution protects established entitlements; it does not supply all the employment terms a claimant wants.

The Fifth Circuit’s expectancy language thus needed narrowing. A personal hope was insufficient; institutional policies and practices must objectively support an entitlement recognized by governing law. Sindermann’s allegations defeated the categorical insistence on formal tenure, without proving he should prevail. If he proved property, he would receive the requested hearing to challenge the grounds for nonretention. The college could still show adequate cause, so reinstatement would not follow automatically.

sources.pinpoint: Rule and Holding; Reasoning; 408 U.S. 599–603 & nn.5–7

sections.title: Some Justices would order process immediately
sections.cue: How much relief did the final judgment actually provide?
paragraphs: Chief Justice Burger joined both Perry and Roth while emphasizing state-law contractual sources. He suggested that uncertain state contract law should first be resolved by state courts through federal abstention. That concurrence did not order Sindermann to initiate separate state litigation before this remand.

Justice Brennan, joined by Justice Douglas, agreed with the speech holding but adopted Marshall’s broader due process position. He would modify the Fifth Circuit’s judgment to direct reasons and an opportunity to respond immediately. Justice Marshall likewise would enter summary judgment for Sindermann’s procedural right, reasoning as in his Roth dissent that government employment decisions must be reasoned and nonarbitrary even absent a separately proved tenure promise. They disagreed with the majority’s requirement of further entitlement proof, not with allowing the speech claim to proceed. Powell did not participate.

On June 29, 1972, the Supreme Court affirmed the Fifth Circuit’s remand, qualified to require a legitimate entitlement rather than subjective expectation. Sindermann could litigate motive and attempt to prove de facto tenure. The Court awarded no damages, declaration of tenure, or reinstatement. Roth had won process below without establishing a protected interest, and the Supreme Court reversed that judgment. Sindermann had lost below without being allowed to prove one. Their opposite summary-judgment positions explain the different dispositions under the same entitlement concept.

sources.pinpoint: Separate Opinions; Judgment; Notes; 408 U.S. 602–605; Roth 587–592
